title: Saʿādat, maʿāli, sumuww: titles at work
goal: At the office, Maryam briefs you before a director general's visit: which title goes in writing, what to call him, and what not to say
tip: Titles go before a post or a name, in writing and formal speech: saʿādat il-mudīr il-ʿāmm, maʿāli l-wazīr. Face to face, the spoken honorific is enough: ṭāl ʿumrak. To check what to say, ask shu nigūl-lah?: shu nigūl-lah fi l-īmēl? 'what do we call him in the email?'
grammar: honorifics: written titles (saʿādat, maʿāli, sumuww) vs the spoken ṭāl ʿumrak
dialogue: A
باكر يزورنا المدير العام من الحكومة، وبو سعيد يبينا كلنا في استقباله
bāchir yzūrna l-mudīr il-ʿāmm min il-ḥukūma, w Bū Saʿīd yabīna killna fi stiqbālah
Tomorrow the director general from the government is visiting us, and Bū Saʿīd wants all of us there to welcome him.
B
زين، وشو نقول له؟ يا شيخ؟
zēn, w shu nigūl-lah? yā shēkh?
OK, and what do we call him? Yā shēkh?
A
لا، هو مب شيخ. في الإيميل نكتب «سعادة المدير العام»، وقدامه نقول طال عمرك
lā, huwa mub shēkh. fi l-īmēl niktib "saʿādat il-mudīr il-ʿāmm", w jiddāmah nigūl ṭāl ʿumrak
No, he isn't a sheikh. In the email we write "His Excellency the Director General", and to his face we say ṭāl ʿumrak.
B
وإذا زارنا وزير؟ نكتب سعادة بعد؟
w idha zārna wazīr? niktib saʿāda baʿad?
And if a minister visits us? Do we write saʿāda too?
A
لا، للوزير نكتب «معالي الوزير». و«سمو الشيخ» للشيوخ من الأسر الحاكمة
lā, lil-wazīr niktib "maʿāli l-wazīr". w "sumuww ish-shēkh" lish-shyūkh min il-usar il-ḥākma
No, for a minister we write "His Excellency the Minister". And "His Highness the Sheikh" is for sheikhs from the ruling families.
B
فهمت. يعني الألقاب في الكتابة والكلام الرسمي؟
fihimt. yaʿni l-alqāb fi l-kitāba w il-kalām ir-rasmi?
I see. So the titles are for writing and formal speech?
A
هيه. وفي الكلام طال عمرك وبس. بس لا تقول له يا ريّال!
hē. w fi l-kalām ṭāl ʿumrak w bas. bas la tgūl-lah yā rayyāl!
Yes. And when you're talking, just ṭāl ʿumrak. But don't call him yā rayyāl!
B
لا تخافين، ولا برو بعد! بكون رسمي من أول ما يدخل
la tkhāfīn, wala brō baʿad! bakūn rasmi min awwal ma yidkhil
Don't worry, and no "bro" either! I'll be formal from the moment he walks in.
A
زين. وخلك على العربي، هو يحب يسمع الشباب يتكلمون عربي
zēn. w khallak ʿala l-ʿarabi, huwa yḥibb yismaʿ ish-shabāb yitkallamūn ʿarabi
Good. And stick to Arabic; he likes hearing young people speak Arabic.
items: (recognise); written before a senior official's post or name
(recognise); for sheikhs of the ruling families
what do we call him? what do we say to him?
to her: shu nigūl-lha? (شو نقول لها؟)
one: il-laqab (اللقب); q kept, as in fuṣḥā
culture: In official UAE writing, titles come before the name and follow fixed rules. Ṣāḥib is-sumuww (His Highness) goes with rulers and members of the ruling families, maʿāli (His Excellency) with ministers, and saʿādat with senior officials such as directors general, ambassadors and members of the Federal National Council. Use sheikh only for someone who really is one.

title: Taking your leave, the old way
goal: In Bū Rāshid's majlis, with Sēf there, hear how visitors entered and left a sheikh's majlis in the old days, and take your leave the same way
tip: Before leaving an elder or a host, ask, don't announce: ṭāl ʿumrak, idha ma shay lāzim, binitrakhkhaṣ 'sir, if there's nothing you need, we'll take our leave'. The host may keep you (igʿid 'stay') or let you go with allāh ywaffigkum, and you answer āmīn.
grammar: taking leave from an elder: ṭāl ʿumrak, idha ma shay lāzim, binitrakhkhaṣ
dialogue: A
أيام أول، إذا رحت مجلس الشيخ، تقول للعسكري عند الباب: أنا فلان بن فلان
ayyām awwal, idha riḥt majlis ish-shēkh, tgūl lil-ʿaskari ʿind il-bāb: ana fulān bin fulān
In the old days, if you went to the sheikh's majlis, you told the guard at the door: I'm so-and-so, son of so-and-so.
B
وهو يدخلك على طول؟
w huwa ydakhkhlak ʿala ṭūl?
And he let you straight in?
A
لا، يستأذن الشيخ أول. والشيوخ يعرفونك من اسم أبوك ويدك
lā, yistaʼdhin ish-shēkh awwal. w ish-shyūkh yaʿarfūnak min ism ubūk w yaddak
No, he asked the sheikh's permission first. And the sheikhs knew you by your father's and grandfather's name.
B
وإذا دخلت، أقعد على طول؟
w idha dakhalt, agʿid ʿala ṭūl?
And once I'm in, do I sit down straight away?
A
لا يا ولدي، ما تقعد لين يقول لك الشيخ تفضل، وما تبدا الكلام قبله
lā yā wildi, ma tigʿid lēn ygūl-lak ish-shēkh tfaẓẓal, w ma tibda l-kalām gablah
No, son: you don't sit until the sheikh says "please", and you don't start talking before he does.
B
وشلون الواحد يطلع؟ ما أبي أطلع بدون ما أستأذن
w shlōn il-wāḥid yiṭlaʿ? ma abi aṭlaʿ bidūn ma astaʼdhin
And how does one leave? I wouldn't want to leave without asking.
A
تقول: طال عمرك، إذا ما شي لازم، بنترخص. والشيخ يقول: اقعد، ولّا الله يوفقكم
tgūl: ṭāl ʿumrak, idha ma shay lāzim, binitrakhkhaṣ. w ish-shēkh ygūl: igʿid, walla allāh ywaffigkum
You say: "Sir, if there's nothing you need, we'll take our leave." And the sheikh says "Stay", or "God grant you success".
B
يلا، طال عمرك، إذا ما شي لازم، بنترخص. الوقت تأخر
yalla, ṭāl ʿumrak, idha ma shay lāzim, binitrakhkhaṣ. il-wagt taʼakhkhar
Right then, sir: if there's nothing you need, we'll take our leave. It's getting late.
A
وين؟ بدري! بس يلا، الله يوفقكم
wēn? badri! bas yalla, allāh ywaffigkum
What, already? It's early! But off you go; God grant you success.
B
آمين يا عمي، الله يحفظك
āmīn yā ʿammi, allāh yiḥfaẓak
Amen, uncle. God keep you.
items: we'll take our leave, may we go now? (respectful)
if there's nothing (else) you need (before taking leave, respectful)
so-and-so, son of so-and-so (how a visitor named himself)
(you) start the conversation, speak first (to a man)
to a woman: tibdīn il-kalām (تبدين الكلام)
they know you by your father's name (to a man)
(recognise); to a woman: yaʿarfūnich min ism ubūch
culture: In the old days, a visitor to a ruler's majlis gave his name at the gate as fulān bin fulān, and the guard asked the sheikh's permission to let him in. The sheikhs knew people by their father's or grandfather's name. Inside, you didn't sit until the sheikh invited you, or speak until he spoke to you, and to leave you asked his permission first.

title: Labbēh, ṭāl ʿumrak!
goal: At the office, your manager Bū Saʿīd calls you in before a meeting: answer the way you answer a senior, take his requests, and offer more help
tip: When an elder or a senior calls your name, answer labbēh 'yes? at your service', not shu?. Take a request with samm ṭāl ʿumrak or ḥāẓir, and offer more: tāmirni ʿala shay thāni? 'anything else I can do for you?'. He may thank you with allāh yirẓa ʿalēk 'bless you'.
grammar: answering a senior: labbēh, samm ṭāl ʿumrak, tāmirni ʿala shay thāni?
dialogue: A
سالم! تعال لو سمحت، أبيك دقيقة
Sālim! taʿāl law samaḥt, abīk dagīga
Sālim! Come here, please; I need you for a minute.
B
لبيه طال عمرك
labbēh ṭāl ʿumrak
Yes, sir?
A
الاجتماع بعد ساعة، والتقرير للحين ما وصلني
il-ijtimāʿ baʿd sāʿa, w it-taqrīr lil-ḥīn ma wiṣalni
The meeting's in an hour, and I still haven't got the report.
B
سم طال عمرك، الحين أطبعه وأييبه لك
samm ṭāl ʿumrak, il-ḥīn aṭbaʿah w ayībah lak
Right away, sir; I'll print it now and bring it to you.
A
وطرش نسخة لمريم بعد، عشان تراجعه قبل الاجتماع
w ṭarrish nuskha l-Maryam baʿad, ʿashān trājʿah gabil il-ijtimāʿ
And send a copy to Maryam too, so she can go over it before the meeting.
B
حاضر. تامرني على شي ثاني؟
ḥāẓir. tāmirni ʿala shay thāni?
Certainly. Anything else I can do for you?
A
وقول للشباب إن الاجتماع بيتأخر ربع ساعة
w gūl lish-shabāb inn il-ijtimāʿ biyitʼakhkhar rubʿ sāʿa
And tell the lads the meeting will start a quarter of an hour late.
B
أبشر، الحين أقول لهم
abshir, il-ḥīn agūl-lhum
Consider it done; I'll tell them now.
A
ما قصرت يا ولدي، الله يرضى عليك
mā gaṣṣart yā wildi, allāh yirẓa ʿalēk
Thank you, son; bless you.
B
ما سوينا شي، هذا واجبي
mā sawwēna shay, hādha wājbi
It's nothing; it's my job.
items: yes? at your service (answering when an elder or a senior calls you)
right away, sir; certainly (respectful) (to a man)
to a woman: samm ṭāl ʿumrich (سم طال عمرج)
anything else I can do for you? (lit. do you order me anything else?) (to a man)
to a woman: tāmrīni ʿala shay thāni? (تامريني على شي ثاني؟)
it's my job, it's my duty, it's the least I can do
I need you for a minute (to a man)
(recognise); to a woman: abīch dagīga (أبيج دقيقة)
she goes over it, she reviews it; you go over it (to a man)
it'll be a quarter of an hour late (a masculine thing)
tell the lads, tell the others (to a man)
to a woman: gūlī lish-shabāb (قولي للشباب)

title: Oops, sorry! Bravo!
goal: At a five-a-side pitch, Rāshid and Sēf react to your game with English interjections; then agree which ones to keep away from Rāshid's dad
tip: With friends your age, borrowed interjections are normal: ūps!, sōri, wāw!, brāvo ʿalēk!, yēs!. With elders, switch to the Arabic ones: is-samūḥa for sōri, yā salām or mā shāʼ allāh for wāw. Rāshid's rule: il-ingilīzi lil-malʿab, w il-ʿarabi lil-majlis.
grammar: borrowed interjections (sōri, ūps, wāw, brāvo) and their Arabic counterparts
dialogue: A
أوبس! سوري، الكورة ضربتك؟
ūps! sōri, il-kūra ẓarbatak?
Oops! Sorry, did the ball hit you?
B
عادي، ما صار شي
ʿādi, ma ṣār shay
It's fine, nothing happened.
A
يلا دورك. واو! شو هالضربة!
yalla dōrak. wāw! shu haẓ-ẓarba!
Go on, your turn. Wow! What a shot!
B
يس! أول هدف لي اليوم
yēs! awwal hadaf li l-yōm
Yes! My first goal today!
A
برافو عليك! سيف، شفت؟ الريّال صار محترف
brāvo ʿalēk! Sēf, shift? ir-rayyāl ṣār miḥtarif
Bravo! Sēf, did you see? The guy's turned pro.
B
لا تبالغ، بس حظ
la tbālig, bas ḥaẓẓ
Don't exaggerate; it was just luck.
A
أوه نو! الكورة طلعت برا الملعب
ōh nō! il-kūra ṭilʿat barra l-malʿab
Oh no! The ball's gone out of the pitch.
B
أنا بييبها. بس قدام أبوك ما بقول سوري، بقول السموحة
ana bayībha. bas jiddām ubūk ma bagūl sōri, bagūl is-samūḥa
I'll get it. But in front of your dad I won't say "sorry", I'll say is-samūḥa.
A
صح، ويقول لك ما عليه. وبدال واو قول يا سلام
ṣaḥḥ, w ygūl-lak ma ʿalēh. w badāl wāw gūl yā salām
Right, and he'll say ma ʿalēh, "no problem". And instead of "wow" say yā salām.
B
فهمت: الإنقليزي للملعب، والعربي للمجلس!
fihimt: il-ingilīzi lil-malʿab, w il-ʿarabi lil-majlis!
Got it: English for the pitch, Arabic for the majlis!
items: (recognise); with elders: yā salām! or mā shāʼ allāh!
bravo! well done! (friends only) (to a man)
he's turned pro, he's become a professional
culture: Young Emiratis switch between Emirati Arabic, fuṣḥā and English every day, and their speech mixes them: Arabic interjections in English sentences, and trendy English expressions in Emirati Arabic. Older people, Emiratis and other Arabs alike, tend to see this mixing as bad Arabic, which is one reason to keep the English for friends.
task: This week: with a tutor or exchange partner (search a tutoring site for «Emirati Arabic tutor»), talk for 10 minutes about a match you watched or played. React the way friends do (sōri, wāw!, yēs!). Then retell the best moment for 2 minutes as if to Bū Rāshid's majlis, with Arabic reactions only (is-samūḥa, yā salām, mā shāʼ allāh).

title: Khaṭīr! Rāshid's new words
goal: Rāshid shows you a video of a new burger place, full of the words young people use now; work out what they mean and who you can say them to
tip: Young people's praise words often mean the opposite of the dictionary: khaṭīr 'dangerous' means 'amazing', mub ṭabīʿi 'not normal' means 'unreal'. Keep them for friends: khallha wiyya sh-shabāb. To calm a friend down, la tṣīr ōvar 'don't go over the top'.
grammar: trendy language: khaṭīr, mub ṭabīʿi, falla, stāyl, ōvar (friends only)
dialogue: A
شوف هالفيديو! المطعم اليديد في الجميرا، البرقر خطير
shūf hal-fīdyo! il-maṭʿam il-yidīd fi l-Jimēra, il-burgar khaṭīr
Look at this video! The new restaurant in Jumeirah: the burger's insane.
B
خطير؟ يعني فيه شي غلط؟
khaṭīr? yaʿni fīh shay ghalaṭ?
Dangerous? You mean something's wrong with it?
A
لا! يعني وايد حلو. والمكان مب طبيعي
lā! yaʿni wāyid ḥilu. w il-makān mub ṭabīʿi
No! It means really good. And the place is unreal.
B
هذي كلمات يديدة علي!
hādhi kalimāt yidīda ʿalay!
These words are new to me!
A
هذي كلماتنا الحين. والجو هناك فلة، والديكور ستايل
hādhi kalimātna l-ḥīn. w il-jaww hnāk falla, w id-dīkōr stāyl
That's how we talk now. And the vibe there is great fun, and the décor's stylish.
B
وأقدر أقول هالكلام لأبوك؟
w agdar agūl hal-kalām l-ubūk?
And can I say this stuff to your dad?
A
لا لا، أبوي بيقول شو هالكلام! خلها ويا الشباب
lā lā, ubūy biygūl shu hal-kalām! khallha wiyya sh-shabāb
No, no, my dad would say "what kind of talk is that!" Save it for the lads.
B
زين، بس لا تصير أوفر، باقي ما ذقناه
zēn, bas la tṣīr ōvar, bāgi ma dhugnāh
OK, but don't go over the top; we haven't tried it yet.
A
خلاص، الخميس نروح كلنا، وانت قول لي إذا خطير ولّا لا
khalāṣ, il-khamīs nrūḥ killna, w inta gūl-li idha khaṭīr walla lā
Fine, on Thursday we'll all go, and you tell me if it's insane or not.
B
اتفقنا! وأنا بحكم على الديكور
ittafagna! w ana baḥkum ʿala d-dīkōr
Deal! And I'll be the judge of the décor.
items: great fun, a great vibe (friends only)
don't go over the top, don't overdo it (friends only) (to a man)
to a woman: la tṣīrīn ōvar (لا تصيرين أوفر)
words that are new to me
save it for the lads, keep it among friends (to a man)
to a woman: khallīha wiyya l-banāt (خليها ويا البنات)
I'll judge, I'll be the judge of

title: Tislam īdak!
goal: At lunch in Bū Rāshid's majlis, with Sēf there, praise the fish he caught, thank him the way guests do, and refuse a third helping politely
tip: Thank a host for food he made with tislam īdak 'bless your hands'; he answers bil-ʿāfya, and you say allāh yʿāfīk. Praise it with ma ʿalēk zōd 'it couldn't be better', and refuse more with allāh la yhīnak, bas shbaʿt. If he says hādha min ṭībak, he is returning the compliment.
grammar: thanks and praise for a host: ma ʿalēk zōd, allāh la yhīnak (recycle: tislam īdak)
dialogue: A
تفضلوا، الغدا جاهز. هالسمك صدته بإيدي الصبح
tfaẓẓalu, il-ghada jāhiz. has-simach ṣidtah b-īdi ṣ-ṣubḥ
Come and eat, lunch is ready. I caught this fish myself this morning.
B
ما شاء الله! تسلم إيدك يا عمي
mā shāʼ allāh! tislam īdak yā ʿammi
Mā shāʼ allāh! Bless your hands, uncle.
A
بالعافية عليك يا ولدي
bil-ʿāfya ʿalēk yā wildi
Enjoy it, son.
B
الله يعافيك. والله ما عليك زود، أحلى سمك أكلته
allāh yʿāfīk. wallāh ma ʿalēk zōd, aḥla simach akaltah
God give you health. Honestly, it couldn't be better; the best fish I've ever had.
A
هذا من طيبك. كل، لا تستحي
hādha min ṭībak. kil, la tistiḥi
That's kind of you. Eat, don't be shy.
B
الله لا يهينك يا عمي، بس والله شبعت
allāh la yhīnak yā ʿammi, bas wallāh shbaʿt
Thank you so much, uncle, but honestly, I'm full.
A
وين شبعت؟ ما أكلت شي! سيف، حط له
wēn shbaʿt? ma akalt shay! Sēf, ḥuṭṭ lah
Full? You've hardly eaten! Sēf, give him some more.
B
لا والله، أكلت وايد. تسلم يا عمي، الله يخليك لنا
lā wallāh, akalt wāyid. tislam yā ʿammi, allāh ykhallīk lana
No, really, I've eaten loads. Thank you, uncle; God keep you for us.
A
الله يسلمك. عيل القهوة! سيف، صب لربعك
allāh ysallmak. ʿayal il-gahwa! Sēf, ṣubb l-rabʿak
God keep you. Coffee, then! Sēf, pour for your friends.
items: it couldn't be better, you can't top that (praise) (to a man)
to a woman: ma ʿalēch zōd (ما عليج زود)
that's kind of you (lit. that's from your goodness) (to a man)
to a woman: hādha min ṭībich (هذا من طيبج)
thank you so much (lit. may God never humble you) (to a man)
to a woman: allāh la yhīnich (الله لا يهينج)
I caught it myself (lit. with my hand) (a fish)
the best fish I've ever eaten
God keep you for us (warm thanks to an elder or a host) (to a man)
to a woman: allāh ykhallīch lana (الله يخليج لنا)
give him some (more) (serving food) (to a man)
(recognise); to a woman: ḥuṭṭī lah (حطي له)
pour (coffee) for your friends (to a man)

title: Same news, office style
goal: At the office, Maryam helps you turn "the report's late, long story" into something you can say in Bū Saʿīd's meeting
tip: In a meeting, keep Gulf grammar but borrow fuṣḥā words, and keep their q: fi l-ḥaqīqa 'in fact', nitwaqqaʿ 'we expect'. Give the reason with bi-sabab + noun, not ʿashān: bi-sabab taʼakhkhur il-bayānāt. With Sēf you'd still say it-taqrīr biyitʼakhkhar, is-sālfa ṭawīla!
grammar: register shifting: everyday → office (fi l-ḥaqīqa, bi-sabab, nitwaqqaʿ; q kept)
dialogue: A
بو سعيد بيسألك في الاجتماع عن التقرير. شو بتقول له؟
Bū Saʿīd biyisʼalak fi l-ijtimāʿ ʿan it-taqrīr. shu bitgūl-lah?
Bū Saʿīd will ask you about the report in the meeting. What will you tell him?
B
بقول: التقرير بيتأخر شوي، السالفة طويلة!
bagūl: it-taqrīr biyitʼakhkhar shwayy, is-sālfa ṭawīla!
I'll say: the report's going to be a bit late, long story!
A
هذا كلامك ويا سيف! في الاجتماع لازم تكون رسمي أكثر
hādha kalāmak wiyya Sēf! fi l-ijtimāʿ lāzim tkūn rasmi akthar
That's how you talk with Sēf! In the meeting you need to be more formal.
B
زين. في الحقيقة، التقرير محتاج أسبوع زيادة
zēn. fi l-ḥaqīqa, it-taqrīr miḥtāj usbūʿ zyāda
OK. In fact, the report needs one more week. (formal)
A
أحسن وايد. وليش؟ لا تقول عشان، قول بسبب
aḥsan wāyid. w lēsh? la tgūl ʿashān, gūl bi-sabab
Much better. And why? Don't say ʿashān, say bi-sabab.
B
بسبب تأخر البيانات من القسم الثاني
bi-sabab taʼakhkhur il-bayānāt min il-gism ith-thāni
Due to the delay in the data from the other department. (formal)
A
ممتاز. والتاريخ اليديد؟
mumtāz. w it-tārīkh il-yidīd?
Excellent. And the new date?
B
نتوقع نسلمه يوم الخميس، إن شاء الله
nitwaqqaʿ nsallmah yōm il-khamīs, in shāʼ allāh
We expect to hand it in on Thursday, God willing. (formal)
A
حلو. شفت؟ نفس الشي، بس بأسلوب ثاني. وفي الإيميل اكتب «نعتذر عن التأخير»
ḥilu. shift? nafs ish-shay, bas b-uslūb thāni. w fi l-īmēl iktib "naʿtadhir ʿan it-taʼkhīr"
Nice. See? The same thing, just in a different style. And in the email write "we apologise for the delay".
B
يعني في المكتب بسبب، وويا سيف عشان!
yaʿni fi l-maktab bi-sabab, w wiyya Sēf ʿashān!
So at the office bi-sabab, and with Sēf ʿashān!
items: q kept in formal talk; everyday speech has g (ma twaggaʿt-ha)
(it) needs one more week, needs another week
in a different style, another way
we apologise for the delay (formal, in writing)

title: You sound like the news!
goal: In Bū Rāshid's majlis, with Sēf there, you answer him in office Arabic; he teases you, and you switch back to majlis talk
tip: Office words sound stiff in the majlis: yitqaddam bi-shakl mumtāz earns you chinnak mudhīʿ akhbār 'you sound like a newsreader'. Switch down to plain talk: ish-shughul zēn, bas fīh ẓaghiṭ wāyid. In a majlis, ma yiḥtāj rasmiyyāt 'no need for formalities'.
grammar: register shifting: office → majlis (recycle: chinnak + noun)
dialogue: A
يا هلا بسالم! شو علومك؟ وشو أخبار الشغل؟
yā hala b-Sālim! shu ʿilūmak? w shu akhbār ish-shughul?
Welcome, Sālim! How are things? And how's work?
B
الحمد لله يا عمي. في الحقيقة، المشروع يتقدم بشكل ممتاز
il-ḥamdu lillāh yā ʿammi. fi l-ḥaqīqa, il-mashrūʿ yitqaddam bi-shakl mumtāz
Thank God, uncle. In fact, the project is progressing excellently.
A
يا سلام! تتكلم كنك مذيع أخبار!
yā salām! titkallam chinnak mudhīʿ akhbār!
My! You talk like a newsreader!
B
السموحة يا عمي، تعودت على كلام المكتب
is-samūḥa yā ʿammi, tʿawwadt ʿala kalām il-maktab
Sorry, uncle; I've got used to office talk.
A
ما عليه يا ولدي. هني مجلس، ما يحتاج رسميات. شلون الشغل صج؟
ma ʿalēh yā wildi. hni majlis, ma yiḥtāj rasmiyyāt. shlōn ish-shughul ṣij?
Never mind, son. This is a majlis; no need for formalities. How's work really?
B
زين، بس فيه ضغط وايد، والمدير دوم مستعيل
zēn, bas fīh ẓaghiṭ wāyid, w il-mudīr dōm mistaʿyil
Good, but there's a lot of pressure, and the manager's always in a hurry.
A
هذا الكلام اللي نفهمه! كلنا جي، الدوام يغير الواحد
hādha l-kalām illi nifhamah! killna chī, id-dawām yghayyir il-wāḥid
Now that's talk we understand! We're all like that; work changes a man.
B
صدقت. في الإيميل فصحى، وفي الاجتماع نص إنقليزي
ṣidagt. fi l-īmēl fuṣḥa, w fi l-ijtimāʿ nuṣṣ ingilīzi
True. Fuṣḥā in emails, and half English in meetings.
A
وفي المجلس؟
w fi l-majlis?
And in the majlis?
B
في المجلس كلام مجالس بس، أبشر يا عمي!
fi l-majlis kalām majālis bas, abshir yā ʿammi!
In the majlis, majlis talk only; you have my word, uncle!
items: q kept, as in fuṣḥā; a feminine thing: titqaddam (تتقدم)
there's a lot of pressure (in it)
work changes a man, the job changes you
majlis talk, the way people talk in a majlis

title: A toast for Bū Khālid
goal: At the office farewell lunch for Bū Khālid, who is retiring after twenty years, give the team's short formal toast and hand him the team's gift
tip: A toast here is a short formal speech, not a drink. Open with yisharrifni + verb and say who you speak for (b-ism il-farīg), praise one quality, and close with a wish: nitmanna-lak it-tawfīq. Formal words keep their q: it-tawfīq, it-taqāʿud, id-diqqa. Then drop back: hādhi hadiyya basīṭa, tfaẓẓal.
grammar: formal speech (toast): yisharrifni, b-ism il-farīg, nitmanna-lak it-tawfīq
dialogue: A
يلا يا سالم، يقولون عندك كلمة!
yalla yā Sālim, ygūlūn ʿindak kilma!
Come on, Sālim, they say you've got a few words for us!
B
يشرفني، باسم الفريق، أقول كلمة بهالمناسبة
yisharrifni, b-ism il-farīg, agūl kilma b-hal-munāsaba
It's an honour, on behalf of the team, to say a few words on this occasion. (formal)
A
تفضل يا ولدي، كلنا آذان صاغية
tfaẓẓal yā wildi, killna ādhān ṣāghya
Go ahead, son; we're all ears.
B
عشرين سنة وانت تعطي هالشركة من وقتك وخبرتك
ʿishrīn sana w inta tʿaṭi hash-sharika min wagtak w khibirtak
For twenty years you've given this company your time and your experience. (formal)
A
الله يخليك، هذا واجبي
allāh ykhallīk, hādha wājbi
Bless you; it was my duty.
B
وتعلمنا منك الصبر والدقة في الشغل
w tʿallamna minnak iṣ-ṣabir w id-diqqa fi sh-shughul
And we learned patience and precision at work from you. (formal)
A
كلامك يرفع الراس يا سالم
kalāmak yirfaʿ ir-rās yā Sālim
Your words make me proud, Sālim.
B
ونتمنى لك التوفيق والصحة بعد التقاعد
w nitmanna-lak it-tawfīq w iṣ-ṣiḥḥa baʿd it-taqāʿud
And we wish you every success and good health in your retirement. (formal)
A
آمين. والله ما توقعت حفلة توديع بهالشكل. ما قصرتوا يا عيالي
āmīn. wallāh ma twaggaʿt ḥaflat tawdīʿ b-hash-shakil. mā gaṣṣartu yā ʿyāli
Amen. Honestly, I didn't expect a farewell party like this. You've all been so kind, my boys.
B
ما سوينا شي. هذي هدية بسيطة من الفريق، تفضل
mā sawwēna shay. hādhi hadiyya basīṭa min il-farīg, tfaẓẓal
It's nothing. This is a small gift from the team; please take it.
items: it's an honour (for me to), I'm honoured (to) (formal)
a few words for this occasion (formal)
you give (some) of your time (to a man)
to a woman: tʿaṭīn min wagtich (تعطين من وقتج)
precision at work, care over detail (formal)
we wish you every success (formal) (to a man)
to a woman: nitmanna-lich it-tawfīq (نتمنى لج التوفيق); q kept
a farewell party, a leaving do
they say you've got a few words (to say) (to a man)
task: This week: record a 2-minute toast (formal) for a friend's graduation or a colleague who's leaving. Open with yisharrifni and b-ism…, praise one quality, and close with nitmanna-lak it-tawfīq. Then record 30 seconds saying the same thing to the friend over karak, the way friends talk: no fuṣḥā words, and as much ḥilu and wāyid as you like.

title: Welcome to our company
goal: At the office, a teacher brings a school group to visit; on Bū Saʿīd's behalf, give a short formal welcome, then switch back to everyday talk for the tour
tip: A formal welcome has three parts: ahlan wa sahlan bikum (the wa is fuṣḥā, kept in this phrase), who you speak for (bin-niyāba ʿan il-mudīr), and yisʿidna + verb 'we're delighted to'. Then drop back to everyday Gulf for the practical bits: il-asʼila fi l-ākhir, yalla yā shabāb.
grammar: formal welcome: ahlan wa sahlan bikum, bin-niyāba ʿan, yisʿidna nraḥḥib fīkum
dialogue: A
السلام عليكم. نحن من المدرسة، عندنا موعد زيارة اليوم
as-salāmu ʿalaykum. niḥin min il-madrasa, ʿindana mawʿid zyāra l-yōm
Peace be upon you. We're from the school; we've got a visit booked for today.
B
وعليكم السلام، حياكم الله! تفضلوا
wa ʿalaykum is-salām, ḥayyākum allāh! tfaẓẓalu
And peace be upon you. Welcome! Come in.
A
الله يحييكم. الطلاب كلهم هني، عشرين طالب
allāh yḥayyīkum. iṭ-ṭullāb killhum hni, ʿishrīn ṭālib
Thank you. The students are all here, twenty of them.
B
أهلا وسهلا بكم في شركتنا. بالنيابة عن المدير، يسعدنا نرحب فيكم
ahlan wa sahlan bikum fi sharikatna. bin-niyāba ʿan il-mudīr, yisʿidna nraḥḥib fīkum
Welcome to our company. On behalf of the manager, we're delighted to welcome you. (formal)
A
الله يحفظك. الشباب متحمسين وايد
allāh yiḥfaẓak. ish-shabāb mitḥammsīn wāyid
God keep you. The boys are really excited.
B
بنبدا بجولة قصيرة في المكتب، وبعدها عرض عن شغلنا
binibda b-jōla gaṣīra fi l-maktab, w baʿdha ʿarẓ ʿan shughulna
We'll start with a short tour of the office, and then a presentation on our work. (formal)
A
ممتاز. ويقدرون يسألون؟
mumtāz. w yigdarūn yisʼalūn?
Excellent. And can they ask questions?
B
أكيد، الأسئلة في الآخر. ونتمنى تستفيدون من الزيارة
akīd, il-asʼila fi l-ākhir. w nitmanna tistafīdūn min iz-zyāra
Of course, questions at the end. And we hope you get a lot out of the visit.
A
إن شاء الله. مشكورين على الاستقبال
in shāʼ allāh. mashkūrīn ʿala l-istiqbāl
God willing. Thank you for having us.
B
العفو. يلا يا شباب، من هني!
il-ʿafu. yalla yā shabāb, min hni!
You're welcome. Come on, lads, this way!
items: the wa ('and') is fuṣḥā, kept in this set phrase
to one man: nraḥḥib fīk; to one woman: nraḥḥib fīch
a visit (booked), an appointment for a visit
for having us, for the welcome

title: Three languages, one meeting
goal: At the office, plan tomorrow's client presentation with Maryam: which parts go in fuṣḥā, which in English, and which in Emirati
tip: Choosing a language is part of the job: il-khiṭāb ir-rasmi bil-fuṣḥa, the slides in Arabic and English, and the talk in Emirati. Technical terms often stay English because some ma lha tarjama wāẓḥa. Ask b-ay lugha? 'in which language?'
grammar: triglossia: il-fuṣḥa for writing, English for terms, Emirati for talk
dialogue: A
العرض باكر للعميل. نسوي الشرايح بالإنقليزي ولّا بالعربي؟
il-ʿarẓ bāchir lil-ʿamīl. nsawwi sh-sharāyiḥ bil-ingilīzi walla bil-ʿarabi?
The presentation for the client is tomorrow. Do we do the slides in English or Arabic?
B
العميل منو؟
il-ʿamīl minu?
Who's the client?
A
جهة حكومية، عشان جي الخطاب الرسمي لازم يكون بالفصحى
jiha ḥukūmiyya, ʿashān chī l-khiṭāb ir-rasmi lāzim ykūn bil-fuṣḥa
A government body, so the official letter has to be in fuṣḥā.
B
والشرايح؟ والكلام في الاجتماع؟
w ish-sharāyiḥ? w il-kalām fi l-ijtimāʿ?
And the slides? And the talking in the meeting?
A
الشرايح بالعربي والإنقليزي، بس الكلام باللهجة. هذا الطبيعي عندنا
ish-sharāyiḥ bil-ʿarabi w il-ingilīzi, bas il-kalām bil-lahja. hādha ṭ-ṭabīʿi ʿindana
The slides in Arabic and English, but the talking in dialect. That's normal for us.
B
يعني ثلاث لغات في اجتماع واحد!
yaʿni thalāth lughāt fi jtimāʿ wāḥid!
So three languages in one meeting!
A
هيه، والمصطلحات التقنية نقولها بالإنقليزي حتى في الاجتماع
hē, w il-muṣṭalaḥāt it-tiqniyya ngūlha bil-ingilīzi ḥatta fi l-ijtimāʿ
Yes, and the technical terms we say in English, even in the meeting.
B
منطقي، لأن بعضها ما لها ترجمة واضحة
manṭiqi, lann baʿaẓha ma lha tarjama wāẓḥa
That makes sense, because some of them have no clear translation.
A
بالضبط. وانت بتقدم الأرقام، بأي لغة؟
biẓ-ẓabṭ. w inta bitgaddim il-argām, b-ay lugha?
Exactly. And you're presenting the figures: in which language?
B
بالعربي، عشان أتدرب. وإذا علقت، الإنقليزي موجود!
bil-ʿarabi, ʿashān atdarrab. w idha ʿligt, il-ingilīzi mawjūd!
In Arabic, for the practice. And if I get stuck, there's always English!
items: fuṣḥā, Modern Standard Arabic (for writing, news and school)
a government body, a government entity
it has no translation, there's no word for it (a feminine or plural thing)
a masculine thing: ma lah tarjama (ما له ترجمة)
if you get stuck (to a man): idha ʿligt (same form)
culture: Emiratis live with three languages. Emirati Arabic is for everyday talk; fuṣḥā is for education, public speeches, literature, Islamic studies and TV news; and English is the common language with people who don't speak Arabic. A young Emirati may chat in Emirati with a friend, read a newspaper in fuṣḥā and switch to English in class, all in one day.

title: On air: why Emirati?
goal: On a university radio programme, the presenter interviews you about learning Emirati Arabic; answer his formal questions in educated Gulf Arabic
tip: On air, structure your answers with educated Gulf linkers: bin-nisba li 'for me', min nāḥya … w min nāḥya thānya 'on the one hand … on the other', bi-shakl ʿāmm 'on the whole'. The presenter's lines are formal (mustamiʿīna l-kirām); your grammar can stay Gulf.
grammar: educated spoken Arabic in an interview: bin-nisba li, min nāḥya … min nāḥya thānya, bi-shakl ʿāmm
dialogue: A
مستمعينا الكرام، أهلا بكم من جديد. ضيفنا اليوم طالب بريطاني يتكلم اللهجة الإماراتية
mustamiʿīna l-kirām, ahlan bikum min jadīd. ẓēfna l-yōm ṭālib brīṭāni yitkallam il-lahja l-imārātiyya
Dear listeners, welcome back. Our guest today is a British student who speaks Emirati Arabic. (formal)
B
أهلا وسهلا، يشرفني أكون معكم
ahlan wa sahlan, yisharrifni akūn maʿākum
Hello, it's an honour to be with you.
A
حدثنا عن تجربتك: ليش اخترت اللهجة مب الفصحى؟
ḥaddithna ʿan tajrubtak: lēsh ikhtart il-lahja mub il-fuṣḥa?
Tell us about your experience: why did you choose the dialect and not fuṣḥā? (formal)
B
بالنسبة لي، الناس هني يتكلمون اللهجة، فحبيت أفهمهم وأسولف وياهم
bin-nisba li, in-nās hni yitkallamūn il-lahja, fa ḥabbēt afhamhum w asōlif wiyyāhum
For me, people here speak the dialect, so I wanted to understand them and chat with them.
A
جميل. وشو أكبر تحدي واجهته؟
jamīl. w shu akbar taḥaddi wājahtah?
Lovely. And what's the biggest challenge you've faced? (formal)
B
من ناحية، حروف مثل العين والحا. ومن ناحية ثانية، الناس يتكلمون بسرعة
min nāḥya, ḥurūf mithil il-ʿēn w il-ḥā. w min nāḥya thānya, in-nās yitkallamūn b-surʿa
On the one hand, letters like ʿayn and ḥā. And on the other hand, people talk fast.
A
وشلون تشوف العربي بين الشباب اليوم؟
w shlōn tshūf il-ʿarabi bēn ish-shabāb il-yōm?
And how do you see Arabic among young people today?
B
بشكل عام، الشباب يخلطون عربي وإنقليزي، بس العربي باقي قوي
bi-shakl ʿāmm, ish-shabāb yikhliṭūn ʿarabi w ingilīzi, bas il-ʿarabi bāgi gawi
On the whole, young people mix Arabic and English, but Arabic is still strong.
A
نشكرك على هاللقاء. مستمعينا، بعد الفاصل نرجع لكم
nashkurak ʿala hal-ligāʼ. mustamiʿīna, baʿd il-fāṣil nirjaʿ lakum
Thank you for this interview. Listeners, we'll be back after the break. (formal)
B
الشكر لكم، والشرف لي
ish-shukr lakum, w ish-sharaf li
Thank you, and the honour's mine.
items: tell us about your experience (formal) (to a man)
(recognise); to a woman: ḥaddithīna ʿan tajrubtich
you faced (it), you came up against (it) (to a man); I faced it
on the one hand: min nāḥya (من ناحية)
we'll be back after the break (formal)
culture: Fuṣḥā is the language of UAE TV news, education and public speeches, but how much of it a speaker uses depends on the occasion and on the speaker's sense of register. It is quite normal to hear Emirati Arabic in a public speech, mixed with some high-register words and fixed phrases taken from fuṣḥā.

title: Off air
goal: Straight after the interview, the presenter drops the formal voice; talk about your nerves, the mixing, and when the interview goes out
tip: The same speaker shifts register in seconds: on air mustamiʿīna l-kirām, off air khalāṣ, ṭilaʿna min il-hawa. Saying what you did on air: ḥassēt inni akhliṭ 'I felt I was mixing', abda bil-fuṣḥa w akammil bil-lahja 'I start in fuṣḥā and carry on in dialect'.
grammar: register shifting: formal → everyday as soon as the mic is off
dialogue: A
خلاص، طلعنا من الهوا. ارتاح يا سالم!
khalāṣ, ṭilaʿna min il-hawa. irtāḥ yā Sālim!
That's it, we're off air. Relax, Sālim!
B
الحمد لله! والله توترت وايد على الهوا
il-ḥamdu lillāh! wallāh twattart wāyid ʿala l-hawa
Thank God! Honestly, I got really nervous on air.
A
ما بان عليك أبد، وصوتك كان واضح في المايك
ma bān ʿalēk abad, w ṣōtak kān wāẓiḥ fi l-māyk
It didn't show at all, and your voice was clear on the mic.
B
بس حسيت إني أخلط فصحى ولهجة في جملة وحدة
bas ḥassēt inni akhliṭ fuṣḥa w lahja fi jumla waḥda
But I felt I was mixing fuṣḥā and dialect in a single sentence.
A
عادي، كلنا جي. حتى أنا أبدا بالفصحى وأكمل باللهجة
ʿādi, killna chī. ḥatta ana abda bil-fuṣḥa w akammil bil-lahja
That's normal; we're all like that. Even I start in fuṣḥā and carry on in dialect.
B
ومتى بتنزل المقابلة؟
w mita bitinzil il-mugābla?
And when will the interview go out?
A
الخميس الياي، الساعة ثمان الصبح، في البرنامج نفسه
il-khamīs il-yāy, is-sāʿa thamān iṣ-ṣubḥ, fi l-barnāmij nafsah
Next Thursday, at eight in the morning, on the same programme.
B
زين، بقول لسيف وبو راشد يسمعونها
zēn, bagūl l-Sēf w Bū Rāshid yismaʿūnha
Great, I'll tell Sēf and Bū Rāshid to listen to it.
A
وإذا تبي، تعال مرة ثانية ونسوي حلقة عن الأكل الإماراتي
w idha tabi, taʿāl marra thānya w nsawwi ḥalga ʿan il-akil il-imārāti
And if you like, come again and we'll do an episode on Emirati food.
B
أكيد! بس هالمرة بتكلم باللهجة من البداية
akīd! bas hal-marra batkallam bil-lahja min il-bidāya
Definitely! But this time I'll talk in dialect from the start.
items: on air, live (on radio or TV)
in a single sentence, in one sentence
I carry on in dialect, (to) carry on in dialect
the interview will go out, will be broadcast
your voice was clear (to a man)
(recognise); to a woman: ṣōtich kān wāẓiḥ
on the mic, into the microphone

title: Fahad hears about the radio
goal: On a video call, Fahad has heard you were on the radio; tell him about it in short, and compare languages at work in Dubai and Kuwait
tip: ṣirt + present verb says something has started happening: ṣirt ansa 'I've started forgetting'. Fahad's Kuwaiti forms (shinu, shdaʿwa, ēh) are for recognition. To sum up for a friend, start with b-ikhtiṣār and list the points.
grammar: triglossia with English: work in English, the majlis in Arabic (ṣirt + verb 'I've started …')
dialogue: A
هلا والله! سمعت إنك طلعت بالراديو! شلون كانت؟
hala wallāh! simaʿt innak ṭilaʿt bir-rādyo! shlōn kānat?
Hey! I heard you were on the radio! How did it go?
B
هلا فيك! كانت حلوة، بس توترت شوي
hala fīk! kānat ḥilwa, bas twattart shwayy
Hi! It went well, but I got a bit nervous.
A
